passages.t: A promise to a woman with no children
passages.happening:
“Again the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD, so He delivered them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years” (verse 1).

In the town of Zorah lives a man of the tribe of Dan named Manoah. His wife cannot have children (verse 2). The angel of the LORD appears to her and tells her that she will conceive and bear a son (verse 3). She is to drink no wine or strong drink and eat nothing unclean. “And no razor shall come over his head, because the boy will be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he will begin the deliverance of Israel from the hand of the Philistines” (verse 5).

She goes and tells her husband that a man of God came to her, whose appearance was like the angel of God, very awesome. She did not ask where he came from, and he did not tell her his name (verse 6). She repeats what he said, and adds one thing: the boy will be a Nazirite to God from the womb ‘until the day of his death’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
This is the last story of a judge in the book, and it opens with the familiar words: Israel did evil, and God handed them over. But one thing is missing. For the first time, Israel does not cry out to the LORD. The people seem to have settled under Philistine rule. The rescue begins from God's side alone.

The Philistines were among the peoples Egyptian records call the Sea Peoples, who came from the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean and settled on the coast around 1200 BC. They lived in five main cities on the southern coastal plain, each ruled by a lord, and they were strong in weapons and war. They pressed east into the low hills where the tribe of Dan had been given land. Zorah and Eshtaol, Manoah's home, lay in the valley of Sorek on that frontier.

Being unable to have children brought grief in that world, and often shame, because children carried on a family's name, worked its land, inherited it and cared for parents in old age. In the Bible a line of women who could not conceive receive a child by God's act: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah, and later Elizabeth. Each time, the child matters at a turning point, and the birth itself shows that God is at work.

A Nazirite was a person set apart to God by a vow. Normally an adult took the vow for a time: no wine or anything from the grapevine, no razor on the head, and no touching a dead body. Samson's case is different in three ways. God imposes the vow. It begins before his birth, so that his mother keeps the food rules while she carries him. And it lasts for life.

The angel's promise is exact. The boy will ‘begin’ the deliverance of Israel. He will not finish it. Samuel and David will carry it on after him.

His mother never gets a name in the story. But she is the one the angel comes to, and she is the one who understands.
passages.later:
The law of the Nazirite is in the book of Numbers: “For the entire period of his vow of separation, no razor shall pass over his head” (Numbers 6:5).

Another mother made a similar promise for her son Samuel: “I will dedicate him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall ever come over his head” (1 Samuel 1:11).

Luke's Gospel echoes this chapter when an angel promises a son to Zechariah and Elizabeth, who had no children: “He shall never take wine or strong drink, and he will be filled with the Holy Spirit even from his mother’s womb” (Luke 1:15).
passages.asks: Israel did not even cry out, and God began to rescue them anyway. Ask what it means for you that God's help can begin before you ask for it. And think of this unnamed woman who could not have children. Ask whom you have overlooked, who may be the one God speaks to first.

passages.t: The angel with a name beyond understanding
passages.happening:
Manoah prays that the man of God will come again and teach them how to raise the boy (verse 8). God listens. The angel comes again, but once more to the woman, sitting in the field without her husband. She runs to fetch Manoah (verses 9-11).

Manoah asks what the boy's rule of life will be. The angel says only that the woman must keep everything he told her (verses 12-14).

Manoah offers to cook a young goat for him. The angel says he will not eat, but they may offer a burnt offering to the LORD. Manoah still does not know it is the angel of the LORD (verses 15-16). He asks the visitor's name, so that they can honor him. “Why do you ask my name,” said the angel of the LORD, “since it is beyond comprehension?” (verse 18).

Manoah offers the goat and a grain offering on a rock, and the LORD does a wonderful thing. As the flame goes up from the altar, the angel of the LORD goes up in the flame. Manoah and his wife fall facedown (verses 19-20).

“We are going to die,” he said to his wife, “for we have seen God!” (verse 22). But she answers calmly. If the LORD had meant to kill them, he would not have accepted their offering, or shown them all this, or told them these things (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The chapter quietly sets husband and wife side by side. Manoah is anxious and always a step behind. He asks for the messenger to come back, but the messenger comes back to his wife. He asks questions the angel has already answered. He wants to feed the visitor and learn his name. His wife, never named, understands more. When he panics, she reasons it through.

Offering a meal to a visitor was the custom of hospitality, as when Abraham welcomed three visitors under the oaks of Mamre. The angel turns the meal into an offering to God.

The angel's name is ‘beyond comprehension’. The Hebrew word belongs to a family of words for wonders that only God can do. In verse 19 the same family is used: the LORD ‘did a marvelous thing’.

Many believed that no one could see God and live. That is why Manoah is terrified. The scene of the angel going up in the flame recalls Gideon, who also offered food on a rock and saw fire consume it (6:19-22).
passages.later:
Abraham, too, welcomed visitors from God with a meal: “Then the LORD appeared to Abraham by the Oaks of Mamre in the heat of the day, while he was sitting at the entrance of his tent” (Genesis 18:1).

The fear of seeing God goes back to Sinai: “no one can see Me and live” (Exodus 33:20).
passages.hard:
Who is the angel of the LORD? Did Manoah really see God?

The chapter uses the words ‘the angel of the LORD’, ‘a man of God’ and ‘God’ almost as if they were the same, and Manoah concludes that they have seen God (verse 22). Similar scenes with Hagar, Abraham, Moses at the bush and Gideon show the same pattern.

Readers give three main answers. Many Jewish and some Christian readers understand him as a created angel who bears God's name and speaks with God's authority, so that meeting him is like meeting God. Many Christian interpreters, from the early church on, have seen him as a visible appearance of God, often identified with the Son before he was born as a man. Others think the messenger is a way of describing God's own presence without claiming that God himself is seen.

These notes take no side. The chapter's point is clear on any reading. God himself began this birth and this rescue, and his presence is both kind and overwhelming.
passages.asks: Manoah's wife saw more clearly than her husband, and the story lets her be right. Ask whose quiet wisdom you have been slow to hear. And hear her reasoning: God would not have shown them all this to destroy them. Ask what God has already shown you of his kindness that should calm your fear today.

passages.happening:
The woman gives birth to a son and names him Samson. “The boy grew, and the LORD blessed him” (verse 24).

“And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him at Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends with high hopes. A child has been promised by God, announced by a heavenly messenger, set apart from the womb, and given the Spirit. No judge has begun so well.

The Spirit begins to stir in Samson before he has done anything at all.

Chapters 14 to 16 will show how far Samson falls short of these hopes, and how God still works through him.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua places Zorah and Eshtaol in the land of Dan: “The territory of their inheritance included Zorah, Eshtaol, Ir-shemesh” (Joshua 19:41).

Of another child set apart from birth, it is said that “the boy Samuel grew up in the presence of the LORD” (1 Samuel 2:21).
passages.asks: Samson began with every gift a person could be given. Ask what gifts and opportunities you were given before you chose anything, and what you have done with them. And ask what it would mean for you to live up to a calling that came to you before you were born.
